reviewer: Consulting botanist review (desk review against POWO, RHS, Go Botany, Dawes Arboretum, Oregon State plant database); field checks still required where noted

top_flags: Count on the 32 rows alone excludes rows 03, 08, 12, 18, 22, 28 (genus only) and treats 23/24 as one unresolved taxon: 23 distinct taxa, BELOW the ArbNet Level I threshold of 25. Adding the 7 map-only taxa reaches 30, but only if those trees are confirmed still standing.
Resolving the six genus-only rows to species would also reach 30 from the 32 rows alone. Realistic combined ceiling is 32 to 33 because the genus rows probably overlap map entries.

Rows 02/11: 'Quercus laevis' is almost certainly Quercus cerris (zone 5-7, naturalized in MA) as the official map says. Q. laevis is a zone 7-9 sandhills tree essentially unknown in New England. Confirm with mossy-bristled acorn cups and whisker-like bud stipules.

Rows 23/24: 'Nothofagus menziesii' (zone 8, evergreen, 1 cm leaves) will not survive a Hingham winter. The official map lists a Fernleaf Beech (Fagus sylvatica 'Asplenifolia') missing from the 32 rows; the silver beech entries are most likely that tree. Check in leaf.
Row 10: no weeping Thuja plicata cultivar is in mainstream trade; the common weeping scale-leaf conifer in New England cemeteries is Callitropsis nootkatensis 'Pendula'. Check cones.

Row 22: Pinus ponderosa was added on the later list only; hardy but rarely planted in the East. Count needles: 3 long flexible with vanilla-scented orange bark = ponderosa; 3 short stiff = native pitch pine; 5 dense = the map's Pinus cembra.

Row 04 vs map-I: inventory says Tamarack (L. laricina), map says Larix decidua. Cones settle it: under 2 cm with 10-20 scales = laricina; 2-4 cm with 30-50 scales = decidua. European larch is the expected 19th-century planting.
Row 15: 'Liberty' is not a seed strain. 'American Liberty' is a multiclone of six vegetatively propagated Ulmus americana cultivars (Elm Research Institute).

Spelling corrections: Quercia > Quercus; Picea abides > Picea abies; Lireodendron > Liriodendron; 'Sangu Kaku' > 'Sango-kaku'; Acer sacharinum > Acer saccharinum; Fagus pendula > Fagus sylvatica 'Pendula'; Fagus asplenifolia > Fagus sylvatica 'Asplenifolia'; Tilia petiolaris > Tilia tomentosa 'Petiolaris'.
Row 29: Acer platanoides is on the Massachusetts Prohibited Plant List (invasive). Keep in the inventory; do not feature as a noteworthy planting; plan no replacements in kind.
Row 09: Catalpa bignonioides vs C. speciosa needs a field check (crushed leaf smells bad = bignonioides; pods under 1 cm wide = bignonioides).
Cercis canadensis (rows 31/32): native to eastern North America but Go Botany treats Massachusetts populations as introduced; label as 'native to the eastern U.S.'.

questions.turkey_oak: Quercus cerris is far more plausible. Q. laevis (American turkey oak) is a small zone 7-9 tree of Southeastern sandhills with no record of thriving in New England; Q. cerris is zone 5-7, a 25-40 m tree, and the Native Plant Trust notes it has naturalized in Massachusetts. Field characters: Q. cerris has buds surrounded by persistent whisker-like stipules, acorn cups densely covered in soft mossy bristles, leaves with mucronate lobe tips and stellate hairs beneath, rough dark fissured bark often with orange in the fissures. Q. laevis has hairless thick deeply lobed 'turkey-foot' leaves, shallow cups with flat scales, no bud whiskers, and rarely exceeds 12 m.
questions.silver_beech: Not plausible. Nothofagus menziesii (silver beech) is an evergreen New Zealand endemic rated USDA zone 8. It would not survive a zone 6b/7a winter in Hingham. The most likely identity is the official map's Fernleaf Beech, Fagus sylvatica 'Asplenifolia' (deciduous, deeply cut narrow leaves, orange-brown fall color). Check in summer: fern-like deeply lobed deciduous leaves 5-10 cm long = 'Asplenifolia'. If genuinely Nothofagus, POWO keeps Nothofagus menziesii; New Zealand authorities use Lophozonia menziesii.
questions.larch: Larix decidua (European larch) is the more common planted larch in a 19th-century cemetery; tamarack is a bog tree rarely sold by Victorian nurseries. L. laricina cones are 1-2 cm with 10-20 scales, needles 1-2.5 cm bluish green; L. decidua cones are 2-4 cm with 30-50 scales, needles 2.5-4 cm bright green, first-year twigs straw-yellow, branchlets drooping. Also rule out Larix kaempferi: cone scale tips curled back.
questions.weeping_cedar: There is no widely grown weeping Thuja plicata cultivar. The two realistic candidates are Callitropsis nootkatensis 'Pendula' (weeping Alaska cedar; synonyms Chamaecyparis and Cupressus nootkatensis), by far the most common weeping scale-leaf conifer in New England cemeteries, and Thuja occidentalis 'Pendula'. Nootka cedar: flattened sprays hanging in vertical curtains, round 1 cm cones with 4-6 pointed scales, resinous smell. Thuja: small oblong cones with 8-12 overlapping scales, sweet tansy smell; T. plicata shows white butterfly marks under glossy foliage.
questions.ponderosa: Pinus ponderosa is hardy to zone 3 so it can survive in coastal Massachusetts, but it is rarely planted in the East and the name appeared only on the later list. Pinus rigida (pitch pine, native on the South Shore) is also 3-needled but with short 7-13 cm stiff twisted needles and persistent prickly cones; Pinus nigra is 2-needled with gray-black plated bark. Real ponderosa has needles 12-25 cm in 3s, yellow-orange jigsaw bark that smells of vanilla, cones 8-15 cm.
questions.liberty_elm: 'Liberty' refers to the American Liberty elm program of the Elm Research Institute (Keene NH), pure Ulmus americana. It is a multiclone of six genetically distinct cultivars selected by Eugene Smalley (University of Wisconsin), propagated vegetatively and shipped mixed. Resistance to Dutch elm disease is moderate. Correct label: Ulmus americana 'American Liberty'.
questions.spellings: Picea abies 'Pendula'; Liriodendron tulipifera; Acer palmatum 'Sango-kaku' (RHS accepted; synonyms 'Senkaki', 'Sango Kaku'); Cornus kousa 'National' (US National Arboretum selection); Cornus florida 'Appalachian Spring' (Catoctin Mountain MD survivor, University of Tennessee 1998); Cercis canadensis 'Appalachian Red' (registered name, originally 'Appalachia'); Acer saccharum 'Green Mountain' (Princeton Nurseries 1964); Fagus sylvatica 'Pendula'; Acer palmatum 'Bloodgood'. Map: Acer saccharinum; Fagus sylvatica 'Pendula'; Fagus sylvatica 'Asplenifolia' (RHS: 'Aspleniifolia'); Tilia tomentosa 'Petiolaris'.

01.origin: Species from Japan, Korea and China; cultivar from Bloodgood Nursery, Long Island NY
01.id_tip: Small tree with 5-7 lobed hand-shaped leaves that stay deep purple-red all summer; the later list drops the cultivar name, so confirm the color holds in July.
01.story: This small maple keeps its wine-red leaves from spring until they flash crimson in fall. It was selected on Long Island from a Japanese garden favorite and planted here to frame the chapel door.
01.confidence_reason: Species certain; cultivar name present on the first list only. Verify summer leaf color.
flags: Cultivar dropped on later list
Distinct from row 27

02.id_tip: Look for acorn cups covered in soft mossy bristles and winter buds ringed by long whisker-like threads; leaves rough, lobes with tiny bristle tips.
02.story: Its acorns sit in shaggy, mossy cups, which is why old gardeners called it the moss-cupped oak. Native to the Mediterranean and Turkey, it was a prized collector's tree in New England's first garden cemeteries.
02.season: fall mossy acorns, winter whiskered buds
02.confidence_reason: Recorded as Q. laevis, a zone 7-9 Southeastern sandhill tree implausible here; the official map's Q. cerris fits climate and history. Needs the acorn-cup check.
flags: Rename from Q. laevis to Q. cerris pending field check
Same taxon as row 11 and map icon A
Spelling: Quercia > Quercus

03.id_tip: Collect a leaf and a winged seed: milky sap from the leaf stalk = Norway maple; silvery leaf underside with deep lobes = silver maple; red stalks and 3-lobed leaves = red maple; U-shaped leaf notches = sugar maple.
03.story: This maple has not yet been named to species, and it may be one of the cemetery's native red or silver maples. A single leaf and seed in June will settle it.
flags: Genus-only row, excluded from the taxa count
May be the official map's silver or red maple

04.accepted_name: Larix decidua or Larix laricina (pending cone check)
04.origin: L. laricina native to Massachusetts; L. decidua native to the Alps and central Europe
04.id_tip: Pick up fallen cones: smaller than a fingertip with 10-20 scales = tamarack; 2-4 cm with 30-50 scales = European larch; curled-back scales = Japanese larch.
04.story: These are conifers that break the rules: they drop every needle each fall after turning bright gold. Eleven of them grow in Section A, one of the largest larch groves in a South Shore cemetery.
04.season: fall color gold, spring soft new needles
04.confidence_reason: Genus certain; species disputed between the inventory (laricina) and the official map (decidua). European larch is the expected 19th-century planting.
flags: Species unresolved: inventory vs official map
Same taxon as map icon I

05.origin: Native to Massachusetts and eastern North America
05.id_tip: Leaves with 7-11 bristle-tipped lobes; bark with long shiny flat ridges like ski tracks; acorns broad with a shallow saucer cup.
05.story: Red oak is the fastest-growing of our native oaks and the one most likely to be standing when the stones around it are gone. Its acorns take two years to ripen and feed squirrels, jays and deer through the winter.

06.origin: Species from northern and central Europe; cultivar of garden origin
06.id_tip: Branches and branchlets hang straight down like a curtain; needles 4-sided and sharp; cones 10-15 cm long, the longest of any local spruce.
06.story: A spruce that grows like a waterfall, with branches that pour down instead of reaching out. Norway spruce is the classic Christmas tree of Europe, and this weeping form was a Victorian favorite for cemeteries because it looks like it is mourning.
06.season: winter evergreen form, long hanging cones
06.confidence_reason: Distinctive and easily verified; spelling corrected from 'abides'.
flags: Spelling: Picea abides > Picea abies

07.origin: Native to Massachusetts and eastern North America
07.id_tip: Five-lobed leaves with smooth U-shaped notches between lobes and no milky sap; seeds in horseshoe-shaped pairs that drop in fall.
07.story: This is the tree on the Canadian flag and the source of maple syrup; it takes about 40 gallons of its sap to make one gallon of syrup. Three of them stand in Section D and turn orange and gold together each October.
flags: Same taxon as map icon M

08.id_tip: Same key as tree 03: snap a leaf stalk for milky sap (Norway), check for silver undersides (silver maple), red stalks and small 3-lobed leaves (red maple).
08.story: A maple still waiting for its name. Volunteers can solve this with one leaf and one seed on a summer walk.
flags: Genus-only row, excluded from the taxa count
May be a second Norway maple (tree 29 notes two in Section D)

09.origin: Native to the southeastern United States; widely planted north
09.id_tip: Huge heart-shaped leaves that smell unpleasant when crushed, pods under 1 cm wide; if the leaf has no smell and pods are over 1 cm wide it is C. speciosa.
09.story: Called the cigar tree for its long bean pods that hang on all winter. In June it is covered in white orchid-like flowers with purple and yellow freckles that guide bees inside.
09.confidence_reason: Genus certain; the two catalpas are often mislabeled and C. speciosa is the commoner planted one in the Northeast.
flags: Confirm C. bignonioides vs C. speciosa

10.origin: Pacific Northwest, Alaska to northern California
10.id_tip: Flat sprays hang in vertical curtains from upswept limbs; round 1 cm cones with 4-6 pointed scales = Nootka; small oblong cones and white butterfly marks under glossy foliage = Thuja plicata; tiny oblong cones with sweet-smelling dull foliage = Thuja occidentalis 'Pendula'.
10.story: Its branches hang like wet green curtains, which made it a favorite mourning tree in Victorian cemeteries. In its Pacific Northwest home this species can live more than a thousand years.
10.confidence_reason: No mainstream weeping Thuja plicata cultivar exists; the weeping scale-leaf conifer usually planted here is Nootka cypress 'Pendula'. Needs a cone check.
flags: Probable misidentification: recorded as Thuja plicata (weeping)

11.id_tip: Same check as tree 02: mossy bristled acorn cups and whiskered winter buds confirm Q. cerris.
11.story: The second of the cemetery's two Turkey oaks, a Mediterranean tree that grows fast and tall. Its shaggy acorn cups look like tiny bird nests.
11.confidence_reason: Same reasoning as tree 02; second specimen of one taxon.
flags: Same taxon as row 02 and map icon A

12.id_tip: Leaves lopsided at the base with double-toothed edges; rough sandpaper leaves = slippery elm; smooth leaves, vase shape, flaky layered bark = American elm; small leaves 2-5 cm = Chinese or Siberian elm.
12.story: Elms once lined every New England main street until Dutch elm disease arrived in the 1930s. Any mature elm still standing is a survivor worth knowing by name.
12.season: fall color yellow, winter vase silhouette
flags: Genus-only row, excluded from the taxa count

13.origin: Species native to Massachusetts and eastern North America; cultivar from a Catoctin Mountain, Maryland survivor, released by University of Tennessee 1998
13.id_tip: Four white notched bracts in May before the leaves; checkered alligator-skin bark; red berries in fall; onion-shaped flower buds in winter.
13.story: When a fungal disease wiped out nearly every dogwood on a Maryland mountainside near Camp David, this one tree kept blooming. Scientists grew copies of it, and that survivor's offspring now flowers here each May.
13.season: spring bloom white, fall red berries and foliage
13.confidence_reason: Named cultivar with documented origin; bracts and bark are easy to confirm.
flags: Susceptible to powdery mildew; monitor

14.origin: Species from Japan, Korea and China; cultivar selected at the U.S. National Arboretum
14.id_tip: Pointed (not notched) white bracts in June after the leaves are out; raspberry-like red fruits in September; mottled bark on older trunks; vase-shaped habit.
14.story: This Asian dogwood blooms a month after our native one, with pointed white petals-that-are-really-leaves and fruits that look like red raspberries. The 'National' form was picked out at the U.S. National Arboretum for its extra-large fruit and upright shape.
14.season: June bloom, September fruit, fall red-purple foliage
14.confidence_reason: Species certain; cultivar name plausible but documentation is thin.
flags: Two trees in Section V

15.origin: Species native to Massachusetts; clones bred at University of Wisconsin, distributed by Elm Research Institute, New Hampshire
15.id_tip: Classic vase shape with arching limbs; leaves lopsided at the base, double-toothed; bark gray in flaky layered ridges.
15.story: After Dutch elm disease killed most of America's street elms, Wisconsin scientists bred six tough strains of American elm and sold them as Liberty elms. This one was planted in memory of Jay Sadler and carries that fight-back story.
15.season: fall color yellow, winter vase shape
15.confidence_reason: 'Liberty' is unambiguous as the American Liberty program; which of the six clones is unknown.
flags: Correct label: Ulmus americana 'American Liberty' (clonal multiclone, not seed-grown)
Monitor for Dutch elm disease; resistance is moderate

16.id_tip: Smooth gray elephant-skin bark; oval leaves with wavy (not toothed) edges and 5-9 vein pairs; long thin cigar-shaped buds.
16.story: Beeches have the smoothest bark of any big tree, which is why people have carved initials into them for centuries. European beech was the signature tree of garden cemeteries like Mount Auburn, and old ones here may date to the 1800s.
16.season: fall color copper, winter smooth gray bark
16.confidence_reason: Distinctive species; American beech differs by toothed leaves with 11-15 vein pairs.
flags: Same taxon as map icon D (different location)
Check for beech leaf disease and beech bark disease

17.origin: Species native to Massachusetts; cultivar from Princeton Nurseries, Kingston NJ, patented 1964
17.id_tip: Sugar maple leaves (U-shaped notches, no milky sap) that are thicker, darker and leathery; neat oval crown.
17.story: A sugar maple chosen in 1964 by a New Jersey nursery for its thick, glossy leaves that shrug off summer heat. It gives the same orange-red fall show as the wild tree but on a tidier, more uniform frame.
17.confidence_reason: Cultivar cannot be verified by eye; accept the planting record. Distinct taxon from tree 07 for ArbNet.

18.origin: Unknown until identified; American holly would be native to coastal Massachusetts
18.id_tip: Dull olive-green spiny leaves and a pyramid shape = Ilex opaca (native); glossy very dark leaves = English holly or a Meserve blue holly; small spineless leaves = Japanese holly.
18.story: Holly keeps its leaves all year and its red berries through the holidays, which is why it has decorated winter homes for two thousand years. American holly grows wild along our coast, and this may be the cemetery's native one.
18.season: winter red berries and evergreen leaves
18.confidence_reason: Genus only. Only female trees bear fruit.
flags: Genus-only row, excluded from the taxa count

19.origin: Species from Japan, Korea and China; cultivar of Japanese origin
19.id_tip: Young twigs and branches coral-red, brightest in winter cold; small 5-7 lobed leaves open pinkish-yellow, green in summer, gold in fall.
19.story: Its name means coral tower in Japanese, and after the leaves fall its bright coral-red twigs glow against the snow. It is one of the few trees here that is at its best in January.
19.season: winter bark coral red, fall gold
19.confidence_reason: Unmistakable winter bark; spelling corrected to the RHS accepted form.
flags: Spelling: 'Sangu Kaku' > 'Sango-kaku'
Section uncertain (V or E)

20.id_tip: Fan-shaped leaves with a notch in the middle, carried on stubby spur shoots; leaves drop almost all at once after turning butter yellow.
20.story: Ginkgo is a living fossil: its relatives grew alongside dinosaurs 200 million years ago and it has no close living kin. It turns pure gold in fall and often drops every leaf in a single day.
flags: Note sex: female trees drop foul-smelling seeds in fall

21.origin: Native to Massachusetts (mainly the Berkshires and hill towns) and northeastern North America
21.id_tip: Flat, blunt needles with two white stripes beneath that leave round flat scars on the twig; smooth gray bark with resin blisters; upright cones that fall apart on the tree.
21.story: This is the classic Christmas tree of the North and the source of the balsam scent in cabin pillows; press a blister on the bark and sticky fragrant resin oozes out. It prefers cool mountain air, so a balsam fir on the coast is a tree living a bit out of its comfort zone.
21.season: winter evergreen scent, spring upright purple cones
21.confidence_reason: Check against Fraser fir and white fir, which nurseries substitute; resin blisters and short needles with round scars confirm.
flags: Short-lived and heat-stressed in coastal zone 7; plan a successor

22.accepted_name: Pinus sp. (recorded as Pinus ponderosa, unverified)
22.origin: Unknown; P. ponderosa is from western North America
22.id_tip: Count needles per bundle: 3 long flexible needles with orange jigsaw bark that smells of vanilla = ponderosa; 3 short stiff twisted needles and cones that stay on for years = pitch pine; 2 needles = Austrian or red pine; 5 stiff needles in a dense crown = Swiss stone pine.
22.story: Ponderosa pine is the great yellow pine of the American West, with bark that smells like vanilla on a warm day. If this tree really is one, it is a rare easterner; if not, it is likely our own pitch pine or the map's Swiss stone pine.
22.season: year-round evergreen, bark scent in summer heat
22.confidence_reason: Identification appeared only on the later list; ponderosa is hardy but rare in the East. Needle count and bark will settle it.
flags: Treated as genus-only until verified
May be the official map's Pinus cembra (icon J)

23.origin: Species from Europe; cultivar of garden origin
23.id_tip: Smooth gray beech bark but leaves narrow and deeply cut into pointed lobes like a fern frond; drops leaves in fall. A true silver beech is evergreen with leaves barely 1 cm long.
23.story: From a distance this looks like a beech; up close its leaves are cut like fern fronds, a quirk gardeners have treasured since the 1800s. It was once mistaken for a New Zealand silver beech, a tree that could not survive a Hingham winter.
23.season: fall color orange-brown, winter smooth bark
23.confidence_reason: Recorded as Nothofagus menziesii (zone 8, evergreen), which cannot persist here; the official map's Fernleaf Beech is otherwise missing from the inventory. Needs a leaf check.
flags: Relabel after inspection
Same taxon as row 24

24.origin: Species from Europe; cultivar of garden origin
24.id_tip: Same check as tree 23: fern-cut deciduous leaves on smooth gray bark = fernleaf beech; if leaves are entire and wavy it is a plain European beech.
24.story: A second tree carrying the silver beech label, in Section C. Whatever it turns out to be, its lacy leaves make it one of the prettiest shade trees on the grounds.
24.confidence_reason: Same reasoning as tree 23; could alternatively be a second plain Fagus sylvatica.
flags: Same taxon as row 23
Probably the official map's icon E

25.origin: Native to eastern North America, reaching southwestern Massachusetts
25.id_tip: Leaves look like a tulip cut off square at the tip; greenish-yellow tulip-shaped flowers with orange centers in June; dry cone-like seed heads stand on the twigs in winter.
25.story: The tallest hardwood in the East, it can top 150 feet in the Appalachians and its straight trunks were carved into dugout canoes. In June it hides yellow-green tulip flowers high in the crown, best seen when they fall to the ground.
flags: Spelling: Lireodendron > Liriodendron
Same taxon as map icon K

26.origin: Japan, Korea, Taiwan and eastern China
26.id_tip: Vase shape like an elm but leaves evenly toothed with each tooth ending in a sharp point and the leaf base nearly symmetrical; bark smooth gray flaking to orange patches.
26.story: Planted across America as a stand-in for the lost American elm, it has the same vase shape but shrugs off Dutch elm disease. In Japan its wood is prized for temple pillars and its fall color runs from gold to rusty red.
26.season: fall color gold to rust, winter mottled bark
26.confidence_reason: Distinctive; easily separated from elm by symmetrical leaf base.

27.id_tip: Hand-shaped 5-7 lobed leaves; note summer leaf color (green vs red), leaf cut (lacy vs plain) and habit (upright vs mounded) to narrow the cultivar.
27.story: The second Japanese maple at the chapel, a different form from its red-leaved partner across the door. Japanese gardeners have named more than a thousand kinds of this one species.
27.confidence_reason: Species certain; cultivar unknown but noted as different from tree 01.
flags: Record summer leaf color and habit to name the cultivar

28.origin: Unknown until identified; American linden would be native
28.id_tip: Heart-shaped lopsided leaves with a leafy strap attached to each flower cluster; big leaves 10-20 cm with tufts beneath = American linden; small 5-8 cm leaves = littleleaf linden; silvery-white felted undersides on drooping branches = silver linden 'Petiolaris'.
28.story: Lindens bloom in early July with tiny cream flowers that bees love; linden honey is a prized European delicacy. Turn a leaf over: silver underneath means this is the cemetery's weeping silver linden.
28.confidence_reason: Genus only. Likely the official map's Tilia tomentosa 'Petiolaris'.
flags: Genus-only row, excluded from the taxa count
Probably the official map's icon N

29.origin: Europe and western Asia; invasive and on the Massachusetts Prohibited Plant List
29.id_tip: Snap a leaf stalk: milky white sap. Leaves broad with 5-7 sharp-pointed lobes; seeds in wide-spread pairs nearly 180 degrees apart; yellow fall color.
29.story: Brought from Europe as a tough street tree, Norway maple seeds itself so aggressively into our woods that Massachusetts has banned its sale. The milky sap in its leaf stalks is the quick way to tell it from our native maples.
29.season: fall color yellow, early spring yellow-green flowers
flags: Invasive in Massachusetts; do not feature on the tour or replace in kind
Also present in Section A

30.origin: Species from Europe; cultivar of garden origin
30.id_tip: Smooth gray beech bark with limbs that arch out then cascade to the ground, forming a green tent you can walk inside.
30.story: A weeping beech makes a living room: its branches sweep to the ground and hide a cool, quiet space inside. These two were planted in memory of Cinda Day and are among the cemetery's most photographed trees.
30.season: summer green canopy tent, fall copper, winter sculptural limbs
flags: Same taxon as map icon C (different location on the map)
Check for beech leaf disease

31.origin: Native to the eastern United States (Pennsylvania and New Jersey southward); Massachusetts populations are treated as introduced
31.id_tip: Pea-like magenta-pink flowers burst straight from bare branches and even the trunk in April; heart-shaped leaves; flat bean pods persist into winter.
31.story: Redbud flowers grow right out of the bark, so in April the whole tree looks dusted in pink before a single leaf appears. It is a member of the pea family and its flowers are edible, with a tart snap-pea taste.
31.season: spring bloom magenta-pink, fall color yellow
31.confidence_reason: Unmistakable in bloom; planted in memory of Sue Bush.
flags: Not a Massachusetts native per Go Botany

32.origin: Species native to the eastern United States; cultivar found by Max Byrkit on a Maryland roadside, released c. 1990
32.id_tip: Like a normal redbud but the April flowers are a hot neon pink-red rather than lavender-pink; compare side by side with tree 31.
32.story: Every redbud blooms pink, but this one was found by a plant lover beside a Maryland road glowing an unusual deep red-pink. A gift of Derby Academy, it blooms a shade brighter than its neighbor in Section A.
32.confidence_reason: Cultivar verifiable only by flower color in April; planting record (Derby Academy gift) supports it.
flags: Originally registered as 'Appalachia'; 'Appalachian Red' is the accepted cultivar name

map-B.origin: Native to Massachusetts and eastern North America
map-B.id_tip: Smooth silver-gray bark; leaves with sharp teeth, one per side vein, 11-15 vein pairs; dead tan leaves cling to young trees all winter.
map-B.story: Our native beech holds its papery tan leaves through the winter, rustling in every breeze. Its small triangular nuts once fed passenger pigeons in flocks that darkened the sky.
map-B.season: fall color golden bronze, winter persistent leaves
map-B.confidence_reason: Official map only, undated; confirm the tree still stands. Beech leaf disease is spreading in Massachusetts.
flags: Not in the 32-row inventory; locate and add
Monitor for beech leaf disease

map-C.origin: Species from Europe; cultivar of garden origin
map-C.id_tip: Beech bark with cascading limbs that reach the ground.
map-C.story: The official map places a weeping beech here, near the Section D and G boundary. Walk under the canopy to see the limbs twist and sweep.
map-C.confidence_reason: Same taxon as tree 30, but the official map puts this icon far from Section B, so it may be a third weeping beech or a map placement quirk.
flags: Spelling on map: Fagus pendula > Fagus sylvatica 'Pendula'
Same taxon as row 30; confirm whether it is one of the two Cinda Day trees

map-D.id_tip: Smooth gray bark; wavy-edged untoothed leaves with 5-9 vein pairs.
map-D.story: The official map places a European beech here in Section A, south of the chapel. These were the showpiece trees of 19th-century garden cemeteries.
map-D.confidence_reason: Same taxon as tree 16 (Section V); this is a different location, so likely a second specimen.
flags: Same taxon as row 16; confirm the tree still stands

map-E.origin: Species from Europe; cultivar of garden origin
map-E.id_tip: Smooth beech bark with narrow leaves deeply cut into pointed lobes, fern-like; fine lacy texture from a distance.
map-E.story: A beech whose leaves are slashed like fern fronds, giving the whole tree a soft feathery look. It is probably the tree the inventory mistook for a New Zealand silver beech.
map-E.confidence_reason: Correctly named on the official map (spelling fixed); likely identity of trees 23/24 but needs a physical match.
flags: Spelling on map: Fagus asplenifolia > Fagus sylvatica 'Asplenifolia'
Probable match to row 24

map-F.origin: Native to Massachusetts and eastern North America
map-F.id_tip: Deeply cut 5-lobed leaves that flash silver underneath in the wind; shaggy gray bark on old trunks; big seeds drop in late spring, not fall.
map-F.story: Its leaves flip silver in a breeze, which is how it got its name. It is the fastest-growing native maple and one of the first trees to bloom, with tiny red flowers in March before the snow is gone.
map-F.season: spring early bloom, summer silver flicker, fall pale yellow
map-F.confidence_reason: Official map only; confirm still standing. May be one of the unidentified maple rows.
flags: Spelling on map: sacharinum > saccharinum
Not in the 32-row inventory; locate and add

map-G.origin: Native to Massachusetts and eastern North America
map-G.id_tip: Something is red in every season: red twigs and buds in winter, red flowers in March, red leaf stalks in summer, scarlet leaves in fall; leaves 3-lobed with toothed edges.
map-G.story: Red maple is the most common tree in Massachusetts and the first to color in September. Look for red somewhere on it in every month of the year.
map-G.season: fall color scarlet, March red flowers

map-H.id_tip: Small tree with small 3-5 lobed leaves with rounded lobes, milky sap in the leaf stalk, corky ridged twigs, and seeds spread flat in a straight line.
map-H.story: In England this little maple is clipped into farm hedges, which is where its name comes from. Its seeds spread out in a straight line like airplane wings, unlike any native maple.
map-H.confidence_reason: Official map only; distinctive enough to confirm quickly if the tree survives.

map-J.id_tip: Five stiff needles per bundle (white pine has soft ones), dense narrow column shape, orange-brown fuzzy young shoots, egg-shaped cones that never open and hold edible nuts.
map-J.story: This slow-growing Alpine pine makes the pine nuts of the Alps, and its cones never open; birds called nutcrackers tear them apart and plant the seeds. It stays tidy and dense for decades, a perfect cemetery evergreen.
map-J.confidence_reason: Official map only; plausible candidate for tree 22 if that pine is 5-needled.

map-N.origin: Species from southeastern Europe; cultivar of garden origin
map-N.id_tip: Drooping branchlets; leaves on long stalks with bright white felted undersides that flash silver in wind; fragrant cream flowers in July.
map-N.story: On a breezy day this tree shimmers silver as its leaves turn over to show their white felted backs. Its July flowers smell of honey and are so rich in nectar that bees sometimes nap beneath it.
map-N.season: July fragrant bloom, summer silver shimmer
map-N.confidence_reason: Map name 'Tilia petiolaris' is an old synonym; RHS and POWO treat it under Tilia tomentosa. Likely the same tree as row 28.
